messages.subject: Questions about Canopy.
messages.body_plain:
Hi

I am Ara Cho, and have a question about Canopy. I use "Sequenza" for copy number calls, and don't  know which one(s) among output of sequenza could be used as a input for Canopy because Sequeza do not gives estimated major or minor copy for Matrix WM and Wm.( Where as it is said that Canopy can directly take the output from Sequenza.) Do I have to calculate WM and Wm using the output of sequenza? If so, could you suggest how to do it?

Thank you in advance.

best,

Ara

messages.subject: Re: [canopy_phylogeny] Questions about Canopy.
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ara,

Thanks for your interest in Canopy! This is a great question and I will update the solution to our GitHub page. Attached is sequenza output from chr11 on one of the samples we have in house. For each CNA region after Sequenza's segmentation, you have the B allele frequency and the depth ratio. Bf = Wm/(WM+Wm) and depth.ratio = (WM+Wm)/2. From here you can solve the WM and Wm.

For example, in the chr11 left arm duplication region, we have Wm/(WM+Wm) =  0.36 and (WM+WM)/2= 1.34. Solving this we have WM = 1.72 and  Wm = 0.96, this checks with the inferred purity 75% and 2+1 allele-specific breakdown by Sequenza (note that Canopy doesn't need the purity or the integer-valued copy number breakdown as input but only the WM and Wm matrix, this is simply a sanity check).

To remove false discoveries in the input (so that it won't be garbage in garbage out for Canopy), we strongly recommend a genome-view across all samples from the same patients and select out the regions that are informative of tree split.

Feel free to let us know if you have any questions. Also we would be very interested in how Canopy works in your dataset. If you don't mind, we would love to hear back.

Cheers,
Yuchao

--
Yuchao Jiang (yuc...@mail.med.upenn.edu)
PhD student in Genomics and Computational Biology
University of Pennsylvania

messages.subject: Selection of variants and CN
messages.body_plain:
Dear Yuchao,
Thanks for the excellent tools you are developping, I'm a happy user of CODEX and have tried Canopy recently. My question is quite general, I was wondering what's the optimal set of variants and allele-specific copy number that should be selected and fed to Canopy?
More specifically, do you need as input a few CNA-free SNAs, other SNAs overlapping with CNAs, and another few CNAs (just as in the breast cancer example in your paper) or is it unnecessary to have all 3 'types' in the set?
Also, it is unclear to me whether WM and Wm need to be provided for all SNAs? (even for cases where falcon segmentation algorithm did not call a CNA? because you might still have a ratio between WM and Wm slightly different to 1:1 at this SNA position).
Again thanks again for your contributions and kind regards,
Vince.

messages.subject: Re: [canopy_phylogeny] Selection of variants and CN
messages.body_plain:
Dear Vince,

Thanks very much in your encouraging feedback! You have a very good question in that how to generate a clean set of input to Canopy is non-trivial. While this is not the focus of our paper, an input with hight false discovery rate will only lead to garbage in garbage out by Canopy. We are currently working on automating the pipeline for both CNAs and SNAs as well as offering guidance to select the informative CNAs. By saying informative, we mean that the SNAs or CNAs show distinct patterns between different samples (from the same patient since we are looking at intratumor heterogeneity). For SNAs, this means that the observed VAFs are different (see Figure 4B in our paper) and in this case a heatmap is a good way for visualization. For CNAs, this means that the WM and Wm are different (see Supplementary Figure S13 in our paper) and IGV is a good tool for visualization.

With this said, you don’t have to have all three types in the mutation input. If you don’t have CNAs, you can feed in Canopy all SNAs. Similarly you can use CNAs only, or a combination of these.

WM and Wm are both for CNAs. The Y matrix specifies whether an SNA lies within a CNA. For SNAs, Canopy doesn’t need a major and minor copy for SNA (which is required by PhyloWGS). For SNAs that are CNA-free, it is possible that the copy number ratio can be different from 1:1 but this might very well be due to false calls by CNA calling software and Canopy doesn’t aim at adjusting for upstream calls.

Hope that this clarifies. I am cc’ing my advisor Nancy here. Nancy, please feel free to add in here.

Cheers,
Yuchao

messages.subject: Re: What is the C matrix?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Soroush,

Thanks for your interest in Canopy. I updated answer to your question on our GitHub page: https://github.com/yuchaojiang/Canopy (see common questions). Basically, if you don’t have overlapping CNAs, you can leave the C matrix as null. If you do have overlapping CNAs however, we recommend manual inspection and visualization of the overlapped events (because given a region, we don’t know from the observed sequencing data how many CNA events there are unless we see different change in copy number or different breakpoint in the same region). The rows of the C matrix are CNA REGIONS and the columns of the C matrix are CNA EVENTS.

Let me know if this clarifies,

Cheers,
Yuchao

> On Sep 28, 2016, at 5:24 PM, Cho, Ara <Ara...@ucsf.edu> wrote:
>
> Hi Yuchao
>
> Thank you for your kind explanation. It really helped,  but still, I have several questions before I run the Canopy.
>
>
> About your recommendation of selecting informative CNV : As you know, Sequenza gives many regions as outputs, and you recommended to use only informative regions among them. Did you mean that I can select the large-continuous regions by MANUALLY inspecting the graph figure?
Yes, I suggest that you do so. I would focus on the large regions (as they tend to be more reliable than small CNAs). Also look across samples to find regions with distinct CNA patterns — these are the events that tell you there is a split along the evolutionary trajectory.
> About epsilonM, epsilonm: What exactly are they and how can I calculate them? In the demo code in github(MDA231), both are pre-fixed to 0.01 while sd(WM) is 0.626 and sd(Wm) is 0.420. Can I use sd(WM) and sd(Wm) when I run Canopy? Or should I fix them to arbitrarily number such as 0.01?

The epsilon is the standard error per CNA event per sample. If you don’t use the default 0.01, it has to have the same dimension of WM and Wm. For example, for CNA1 in sample1, we call the major and minor ratio at many heterozygous loci in a region. The sd is calculated across all these loci for this event in this sample. Basically it tells Canopy how confident you are of the CNA input. sd(WM) and sd(Wm) give the standard deviations of all CNAs across all samples. I haven’t thought too much about generating this using the sequenza output since we are mostly using Falcon-X in our lab. I feel the default 0.01 is fairly reasonable.

> About matrix C: Even if multiple CNA regions exist in the same chromosome, the matrix C is not necessary as long as they are not overlapped each other, is that correct?
>
>
This is correct. I've also further elaborated on this in our GitHub page under common questions.

> Thank you in advance.

> Best,
